doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Learning melodies: his father's assignment on Bourbon Street Parade
summary: Brunious stresses learning melodies; his father had him learn Bob Thomas's solo from a Paul Barbarin record.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: And what timing man. That’s one thing that you could get from Louis Armstrong, listening to him. The timing. Because I mean, you know, he had it. He created it basically. But anyway. What else do you talk about after Louis Armstrong? Louis Armstrong is God I guess. Also, when you were saying with the young players, when he was asking about trying to get them, what would you advise them about learning to play jazz, and you made such a strong statement about learning melodies. Because and you even said this about when you play a solo, it’s just another melody. That’s all it is. A melody, by my definition — and Webster didn’t have anything to do with this one — but I thought it was kind of think of it as a series of notes that tie some changes together. And that’s basically what a solo is.

So I mean to learn melodies, which I don’t think we accentuate upon them enough in the schools. I mean my dad had recorded a record with Paul Barbarin in the 1950s and one of the cuts on there was “Bourbon Street Parade” which Paul Barbarin wrote. And what my dad used to do was he’d tell us, “I’m going out for a while, and I want you to learn like Bob Thomas’ solo on ‘Bourbon Street Parade.’” And as a result of that I can hum that solo right now, you know? That had that kind of impact on me. And you know I mean I’m not a real older style player, in fact still, it’s in me.
Well I mean, but it’s like you know that’s really maturing type of tactics and things to do that help you to mature faster. I think so.
